q: The phenomenon that is nearly opposite of habituation is termed:

concept.t: Habituation is a decrease in responding to a repeated, harmless stimulus.
Sensitisation is an increase in responding, usually to many stimuli, after a strong or noxious one (Section 6.1).
Only sensitisation is a real learning term here; the other three options are not learning terms at all.

wrong.b: Not a learning term; a filler distractor with no meaning in learning theory.
wrong.c: Not a learning term; a sound-alike distractor built to look like habituation.
wrong.d: Not a learning term; a sound-alike distractor one syllable short of habituation.

q: In Pavlov's experiment with dogs, the sound of the bell/metronome was the:

concept.t: The metronome alone does not produce salivation, so it is a neutral stimulus.
Once paired with food, it produces salivation on its own, so it is now a conditioned stimulus.
Food, not the bell, is the unconditioned stimulus.

wrong.a: "Operant stimulus" is not a term of classical conditioning; the label borrows operant language.
wrong.c: Food, not the bell, is the unconditioned stimulus; before pairing the bell produces no salivation.
wrong.d: Reverses the order: the bell is neutral first and becomes conditioned only after pairing.

q: Which of the following is most effective in conditioning?

concept.t: In delay conditioning the CS begins first and is still present when the UCS arrives.
The CS serves as a warning that the UCS is coming, so it predicts it most clearly.

wrong.a: Backward conditioning presents the UCS before the CS; it is the least effective and often makes the CS a signal of safety.
wrong.c: Simultaneous conditioning starts CS and UCS together, so the CS gives no advance warning.
wrong.d: Trace conditioning leaves a gap between the CS and the UCS, so it is weaker.

q: A child has learned to avoid a furry, black cat. However, she still plays with her grandmother's short-haired tabby. Her response demonstrates:

concept.t: Discrimination is responding differently to similar stimuli.
She avoids the furry black cat but still plays with the short-haired tabby, so her fear is limited to one kind of cat.
Generalisation would be fearing every cat that resembles the black one.

wrong.b: Extinction would mean the learned fear has faded, but her fear of the black cat has not gone.
wrong.c: Successive approximation is shaping, reinforcing closer and closer steps towards a target behaviour; nothing is being shaped here.
wrong.d: Negative transfer is earlier learning hindering new learning (Section 6.10), not a pattern of responding to similar stimuli.

q: In reinforcement learning, the "prediction error" signal in the brain is primarily associated with:

concept.t: Schultz found that dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra fire to an unexpected reward.
With learning, the firing shifts to a cue that predicts the reward, and it dips when a predicted reward fails to arrive.
That pattern is the prediction error of the Rescorla-Wagner model (Section 6.4).

wrong.a: Serotonin is linked mainly to mood, sleep and appetite; it does not carry the prediction error signal.
wrong.c: GABA is the brain's main inhibitory transmitter; it does not carry the prediction error signal.
wrong.d: Acetylcholine works at the neuromuscular junction and in attention and memory; it does not carry the prediction error signal.

q: Taste aversion is an example of:

concept.t: The taste is the CS and the illness the UCS.
They are paired once, often hours apart, yet the aversion still forms; it is also called the Garcia effect.

wrong.b: Second-order conditioning uses an established CS to condition a new one; no such CS is used here.
wrong.c: Operant conditioning needs a response that is reinforced; no response is reinforced here.
wrong.d: Spurious association is a statistical term, not a type of learning.

q: Systematic desensitization technique is based upon the idea of:

concept.t: Reciprocal inhibition: two incompatible responses cannot occur together, so a calm response suppresses anxiety.
Wolpe paired each step of an anxiety hierarchy with relaxation, a response incompatible with anxiety (Section 6.4).

wrong.b: The law of effect is Thorndike's operant principle, not the idea behind desensitisation.
wrong.c: Habituation underlies exposure and response prevention, not systematic desensitisation.
wrong.d: Adaptation to stress belongs to stress theory (Chapter 11), not to this therapy.

q: Exposure and response prevention procedure is based on behaviour therapy principal of:
who: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) for OCD

concept.t: The client meets the obsessional cue and is prevented from performing the compulsion.
The anxiety rises, peaks and falls without the escape response, which is habituation and extinction at work.

wrong.a: Counterconditioning trains an incompatible response, as in systematic desensitisation; no incompatible response is trained in ERP.
wrong.c: Reciprocal inhibition also describes systematic desensitisation, which trains an incompatible response; ERP trains none.
wrong.d: Graded exposure is a way of presenting stimuli, not the learning principle behind the change.

q: The "law of effect," formulated by Edward Thorndike, states that:

concept.t: Responses followed by satisfaction are strengthened; those followed by discomfort are weakened (Section 6.5).
Thorndike's cats in puzzle boxes escaped faster over trials as the successful response was stamped in.

wrong.b: Bandura's observational learning, learning by watching models, not from one's own consequences.
wrong.c: Köhler's insight, a sudden restructuring of the problem, not learning from consequences.
wrong.d: Freud's idea of unconscious drives, not a learning principle.

q: The behavioral technique that involves removing a desirable stimulus following an undesirable behavior in order to reduce the frequency of that behavior is called:

concept.t: Response cost removes a desirable stimulus after an undesirable behaviour, to reduce that behaviour.
It is a form of negative punishment: negative means something is taken away, punishment means the behaviour decreases.
Losing tokens or paying a fine for misbehaving.

wrong.a: Negative reinforcement removes something to increase behaviour; the trap is reading "negative" as punishment.
wrong.c: Positive punishment adds something unpleasant; response cost takes something away.
wrong.d: Extinction simply stops delivering the reinforcer that maintained the behaviour; nothing the person already has is taken.

q: The first-grade teacher gives students stickers when they perform well. If they earn five stickers in one day they are exempt from homework. The stickers in this example could also be called:

concept.t: A token is exchanged for a backup reinforcer; here, five stickers buy exemption from homework.
Stickers used this way are secondary reinforcers, valued for what they buy, not primary ones.

wrong.a: A primary reinforcer satisfies a biological need, like food or water; stickers matter only for what they buy.
wrong.c: A generalised reinforcer buys many different backups (money), whereas these stickers buy only one.
wrong.d: A prepotent response is a dominant response, not a reinforcer.

q: A parent deliberately ignores a child's temper tantrums in an attempt to discourage them. The parent's strategy is in accordance with:

concept.t: Extinction means withholding the reinforcer that maintained a behaviour, so the behaviour fades.
Ignoring withholds the attention that reinforced the tantrums (Williams, 1959; Section 6.5).
The source key marks (c), but that is wrong; the correct answer is extinction.

wrong.a: Negative reinforcement would increase behaviour, not discourage it.
wrong.c: Escape terminates an aversive stimulus; the source key marks this, but ignoring a tantrum is not escape.
wrong.d: Avoidance prevents an aversive stimulus; ignoring a tantrum prevents nothing aversive.

q: A client with OCD washes their hands excessively to neutralize the anxiety caused by intrusive thoughts of contamination. This hand-washing behavior is BEST conceptualized as a(n):

concept.t: In Mowrer's two-factor theory, fear is learned by classical conditioning and avoidance is kept going by operant conditioning.
Washing reduces anxiety and is therefore negatively reinforced: the second factor (Section 6.5).

wrong.a: Washing is a learned response, not a stimulus.
wrong.b: Washing is learned, so it is not an unconditioned response.
wrong.d: It is maintained by the removal of anxiety, not by positive reinforcement.

q: Sheena is studying for her final exam in her psychology class. For every 45 minutes that she studies, she gives herself a mini chocolate, then goes back to studying. What Schedule of reinforcement is Sheena using?

concept.t: The requirement is a constant amount of time, not a number of responses (ratio) and not an unpredictable period (variable).
Strictly, reward after a fixed time regardless of responding is a fixed-time arrangement, but among these options fixed interval is correct (Section 6.6).

wrong.a: Variable ratio rewards after an unpredictable number of responses; Sheena's reward depends on time.
wrong.b: Variable interval uses an unpredictable period; Sheena's 45 minutes is constant.
wrong.d: Fixed ratio rewards after a set number of responses, not a set amount of time.

q: Among the following schedules of reinforcement, which typically produces the highest rate of response and is most resistant to extinction?

concept.t: Ratio schedules reward fast responding: more responses bring more rewards.
Unpredictability removes any reason to pause and makes it hard to detect that reinforcement has stopped, so it resists extinction.
Slot machines work this way.

wrong.a: Fixed ratio produces pauses after reinforcement, so its rate is not the highest overall.
wrong.c: Fixed interval produces a scallop: little responding just after reward, speeding up as the interval ends.
wrong.d: Variable interval produces only a moderate rate.

q: According to the Premack Principle, a high-probability behavior (for example, playing video games) can be used to:

concept.t: A more preferred activity, made available only after a less preferred one, reinforces the less preferred one.
It is called grandma's rule: eat your vegetables, then you get dessert (Section 6.6).

wrong.c: It runs from high to low probability, not between two high-probability activities.
wrong.d: The principle concerns reinforcement, not extinction.

q: Learned helplessness phenomenon is offered by:

concept.t: Seligman and Maier's yoked dogs were given inescapable shock.
Later they failed to escape avoidable shock: they had learned that nothing they did mattered, which is learned helplessness (Section 6.6).

wrong.a: Beck is known for the cognitive triad of depression; the trap is that helplessness is also linked to depression.
wrong.c: Sullivan is known for interpersonal theory.
wrong.d: Kahneman is known for heuristics and biases.

q: The Crespi effect in learning experiments refers to:

concept.t: Crespi's rats shifted from a small to a larger reward ran faster than rats always given the larger reward: positive contrast.
The reverse shift, from large to small, produced negative contrast.
The changes were too abrupt to be learning, so they reflect motivation (Section 6.6).

wrong.a: Describes memory interference, not a reward effect.
wrong.c: Describes extinction, not a change in reward size.
wrong.d: Describes Köhler's insight, not a reward effect.

q: The technique that is based on the idea that the autonomic nervous system can come under voluntary control through operant conditioning is known as:
who: Miller, biofeedback (operant control of autonomic responses)

concept.t: A bodily process is measured and displayed, so changes in the desired direction are reinforced by the feedback.
Miller argued that autonomic responses can be operantly conditioned (Section 6.6).

wrong.b: Hypnosis is an altered state (Chapter 5), not operant conditioning.
wrong.c: Sublimation is a Freudian defence mechanism.
wrong.d: Systematic desensitisation is a classical counterconditioning technique, not operant.

q: What is the main difference between classical and operant conditioning?

concept.t: Classical conditioning associates two stimuli, such as bell and food.
Operant conditioning associates a response with its consequences, reinforcement and punishment (Table 6.9).

wrong.c: False, because classical conditioning depends on prediction (Rescorla), a cognitive process.
wrong.d: Ignores how constantly the two interact, as in two-factor theory and autoshaping.

q: Latent learning was demonstrated by:

concept.t: Tolman and Honzik's rats found food in the maze only from day 11, yet immediately performed as well as rats rewarded throughout.
They had learned the maze without reward and showed it once a reason appeared: latent learning (Section 6.7).

wrong.c: Skinner is operant conditioning.
wrong.d: Köhler is insight.

q: Concept formation stages include the following:

concept.t: The learner observes instances, then discriminates them from non-instances.
Next the learner generalises to all instances sharing the essential features, and abstracts the defining properties (Section 6.7).

wrong.b: Includes assimilation, which is Piaget's term, not a stage of concept formation, and starts with abstraction, the last stage.
wrong.c: Puts generalisation before discrimination; the order is the trap.
wrong.d: Includes assimilation, Piaget's term, not a stage of concept formation.

q: According to Albert Bandura, which of the following is NOT a necessary component process for observational learning to occur?

concept.t: The four processes are attention, retention, motor reproduction and motivation.
The 1965 Bobo doll study showed that children learn a model's behaviour whether or not anyone is reinforced.
Reinforcement affects only whether the behaviour is performed, not whether it is learned (Section 6.8).

wrong.a: True component: attention to the model comes first; without it nothing is learned.
wrong.b: True component: motivation decides whether the learned behaviour is actually performed.
wrong.d: True component: motor reproduction turns the remembered behaviour into action.

q: Reciprocal causation model has been described under:

concept.t: Bandura's triadic reciprocal causation (reciprocal determinism) holds that person, behaviour and environment influence one another (Section 6.8).
It is the core of his social cognitive theory.

wrong.c: Drive-reduction theory is Hull's.
wrong.d: Constructivism (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner) concerns how learners build knowledge (Section 6.9).

q: Learning always leads to efficacy, provided presence of a significant factor which is:

concept.t: Locke and Latham showed that specific, difficult goals, together with knowledge of results, direct attention, mobilise effort and increase persistence.
With a goal, practice becomes purposeful, so learning turns into effective performance (Section 6.10).

wrong.a: Ability helps, but on its own it does not turn learning into effective performance.
wrong.b: Aptitude helps, but on its own it does not turn learning into effective performance.
wrong.c: Knowledge helps, but on its own it does not turn learning into effective performance.
